Microfluidic mold or chip Our layout is shown in Figure 1 , and a mask design for photolithography is provided as supplementary information (see Co-culture chip.zip. Design files for a microfluidic chip for co-culturing different species of bacteria. The chip includes several different trap designs and geometries to facilitate experiment optimization). The specific design of a microfluidic chip is not critical, but some key considerations are as follows: Trapping regions should be large enough to contain enough cells to make interesting dynamics likely, but they should also be small enough to allow sufficient diffusion of nutrients throughout the trap. We used several trap geometries with areas on the order of 10 4 μm 2 . Trap heights should maintain a cell monolayer. We used approximately 0.8-1 μm. The fluid channels should avoid right angles and dead spaces, which contribute to clogging. Note: Our chip was based on the design developed in Danino et al. (2010), with parallel main media channels that have trapping chambers on their sides. We included multiple trap geometries, including some with one edge open to media channels, some with two edges open, some with additional, low-flow wings, and some with media feeder channels at the back, so we could test them all in parallel ( Figure 2 ). The chip also includes a Dial-A-Wave design that allows precise control of the ratios of two different media sources. For single-media experiments as described here, it is sufficient to only use one inlet port, leaving the others un-punched. For further design considerations and details on media switching, see Ferry et al. (2011). If you have a pre-fabricated chip, you do not need items 1-16, and items 18-21 may need to be adjusted as appropriate for use with your chip. Figure

A microfluidic chip with four rows of traps and 3 media ports to allow dynamic media switching. Channels shown in blue are 20 μm tall, traps shown in green are 0.8-1 μm tall, and an optional layer of feeder channels shown in red are 0.2 μm tall. The three inlets allow precise concentrations of a dynamically varying chemical of choice, via the Dial-A-Wave mechanism. Note that the feeding channel layer and use of more than one inlet are optional. Figure

A closer view of the four rows of trapping regions. A. The top row contains 100 μm wide traps that alternate between 100 and 200 μm long, open to channels on two sides. B. The second row contains the same trap design with additional wings on the side that experience lower flow. C. The third row of traps is the same as the first, but open on only one side. D. The fourth row of traps is the same as the third, but the back is connected to another media channel by an optional third 0.2 μm tall layer to allow media exchange without allowing cells through. Note that this very low-height layer is technically difficult both to fabricate on a wafer (mold) and to prevent from collapsing on an assembled PDMS chip. Another option would be to use a plasmid with the ColE1 origin of replication, which cannot propagate in A. baylyi, but to insert a GFP gene (and optionally the antibiotic resistance marker) between two flanking regions of A. baylyi genomic homology. This would encourage homologous recombination into the A. baylyi genome, which occurs at higher frequency than transfer of a self-replicating plasmid ( Palmen et al., 1993 ). A good strain of E. coli for use in microfluidics is MG1655 (Coli Genetic Stock Center, catalog number: 6300), although other strains will work as well. Common cloning strains with mutations in recA, including dh5-alpha, are not ideal because they grow more slowly. steps.title: Mix PDMS components
steps.instruction: Weigh 36.4 g Sylgard 184 PDMS base (Ellsworth Adhesives, cat 184 SIL ELAST KIT 0.5KG) and 3.6 g curing agent into a plastic weighing boat (Fisher Scientific, cat 12‑640) and stir thoroughly with a glass stir bar.

steps.title: Degas PDMS mixture
steps.instruction: Place the PDMS mixture in a vacuum desiccator; apply vacuum until bubbles rise to the surface, briefly release vacuum to pop bubbles, then re‑apply vacuum until no bubbles remain.

steps.title: Prepare wafer and mold
steps.instruction: Wrap the wafer containing trap molds with a sheet of aluminum foil (Reynolds Recycled, cat B0028LZ86A) and press gently with a clean plastic weighing boat to remove trapped air without contacting the mold features.

steps.title: Pour PDMS onto wafer
steps.instruction: Pour the degassed PDMS onto the prepared wafer, return the assembly to the vacuum desiccator for a second degassing step, then cure at 80 °C in an oven for 1 h (or overnight). Allow the cured PDMS to cool to room temperature before proceeding.

steps.title: Cut and punch chip ports
steps.instruction: Peel the cooled PDMS slab from the wafer, cut individual chips on a cutting mat (Harris, cat WB100020) with a razor blade (Fisher Scientific, cat 12‑640), and flip each chip feature‑side up under a dissecting microscope. Use a 0.5 mm biopsy punch (World Precision Instruments, cat 504528) to punch a core through each desired media port (one inlet and one outlet for single‑media experiments).

steps.title: Clean chips and coverslips
steps.instruction: Sequentially rinse chips with 70 % ethanol (Fisher Scientific, cat BP8201500) then distilled water, drying with a nitrogen gas stream; flush ports with high‑velocity nitrogen or inject 70 % ethanol/water through them using a syringe and luer‑stub adapter. Immediately cover chip surfaces with clear removable tape (Scotch Magic Tape, cat B0000DH8HQ). In a fume hood, clean #1.5 glass coverslips (Fisher Scientific, cat 12‑530F) with heptane, then methanol (Fisher Scientific, cat A412‑500), then distilled water, drying with nitrogen and taping them to prevent dust.

steps.title: Oxygen plasma activation and bonding
steps.instruction: Place chips (feature side up) and taped coverslips in a UVO cleaner, open the oxygen line, and expose for 3 min. Close the oxygen valve, peel off the tape, then bring each chip feature‑side down onto its coverslip. Bake the assembled devices at 80 °C for 1 h (or overnight) to complete bonding. For chips with low‑height (≈1 µm) traps, place the coverslip on top of the chip to avoid collapse.

steps.title: Prepare syringes and tubing
steps.instruction: Gather BD 60 ml Luer‑Lok syringes (cat 309053), 0.02 in ID / 0.06 in OD Tygon tubing (cat AAD04103), straight 23 ga × 0.50 in luer stubs (Instech, cat LS23S), and bent 23 ga × 0.50 in 90° luer stubs (OK International, cat 923050‑90BTE). Soak each bent stub in acetone to dissolve the plastic, pull out the metal piece with tweezers, discard the plastic, and keep the metal. Attach a straight stub to a 50 ml syringe, connect a length of tubing, and insert the metal piece from the bent stub into the opposite end of the tubing.

substeps.instruction: Prime each tubing (except one) by injecting 1 ml LB + Tween 20 (see Recipe 2) through the syringe bottom, then add an additional 10 ml LB + Tween 20, allow bubbles to escape, tape the tubing just above the liquid level, and seal the syringe top with tape or parafilm (Bemis, cat PM996).
Use room‑temperature media; if media were chilled, let it warm to ≥ room temperature before loading.

steps.title: Prepare LB + Tween 20 media (Recipe 2)
steps.instruction: Dissolve 25 g LB powder (BD, cat 244610) in distilled water and bring the volume to 1 L; add Tween 20 (Sigma‑Aldrich, cat P9416‑50ML) to the desired final concentration (as used for priming). Filter‑sterilize the solution.

steps.title: Grow and wash bacterial cultures
steps.instruction: Inoculate 10–15 ml of each strain in LB containing the appropriate antibiotic (kanamycin 50 µg ml⁻¹ for E. coli carrying pBAV1k‑GFP; spectinomycin 17 µg ml⁻¹ for A. baylyi with chromosomal mCherry) and grow to mid‑exponential phase. Transfer cultures to 15 ml conical tubes and centrifuge 5 min at 2,000 × g (room temperature). Resuspend pellets in 1 ml fresh LB, move to 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tubes, and centrifuge 3 min at 10,000 × g. Remove supernatant and resuspend each pellet in 1–3 volumes LB + Tween 20 per pellet volume.

substeps.instruction: Mix the two strains at a ratio of 3 vol E. coli : 1 vol A. baylyi (adjustable depending on strain adhesiveness).

steps.title: Load cell mixture into syringe
steps.instruction: Transfer the prepared cell suspension into a fresh 60 ml Luer‑Lok syringe with tubing using the same priming procedure as for media syringes.

steps.title: Connect syringes to chip and start flow
steps.instruction: Insert each media syringe luer stub into its corresponding chip inlet (lower stub below fluid level, wait for flow, then insert). Insert the cell‑loaded syringe into the waste port. Optionally place the chip in a vacuum desiccator for ≥ 20 min before loading to improve filling.

substeps.instruction: Mount the chip on the microscope stage, secure it, and raise the syringes several feet above the chip (tape them to the wall if needed).
Adjust syringe heights so that media and cells meet roughly midway in the trapping region; then set a slow forward flow from media inlet to waste.
If cells do not load well, gently flick the waste line with a finger, increasing force as needed, to generate pressure waves that push cells into traps (avoid pushing cells into upstream channels).

steps.title: Optimize flow after loading
steps.instruction: Once traps contain sufficient cells, fine‑tune syringe heights to maintain a forward flow that is fast enough to prevent clogging but gentle enough to retain the less‑sticky E. coli in the traps. Adjust flow rates upward as cells grow and fill traps.

substeps.instruction: If cells wash out, raise the waste syringe or lower the media syringe to reduce flow.
If clogging begins, lower the waste syringe or raise the media syringe to increase flow; occasional flicking of tubing can temporarily relieve clogs.

steps.title: Set up time‑lapse imaging
steps.instruction: Configure the microscope to acquire one image set every 3–5 min, using the lowest exposure that still yields reliable fluorescence (prefer longer exposure at lower intensity). Use a motorized stage to image multiple positions if possible. Monitor the experiment, adjusting flow as described above to keep cells growing and channels clear.
